blocks.text: Prabowo's statement in Gorontalo was not just an explosion of political emotion. It was part of a communication architecture that he had built for over a decade.
When the fishermen are often forgotten, smart people in Jakarta don't care about the fate of the fishermen. Change now.

The President of Prabowo Subianto's statement, pronounced in the presence of the Gorontalo fishermen on May 9, 2026, soon spread widely across social media and national news channels. But the main focus is not whether that statement is right or wrong. The more important question is: why would a president choose that prediction, in that place, in that moment.
The answer shows something bigger than just sympathy for fishermen. It shows a pattern of consistent, strategic, political communication and very conscious public psychology.

For over a decade, Prabowo built his political identity through one great line of narrative: people of the region versus central elite. In various campaign speeches or state statements, he repeatedly placed farmers, fishermen, and laborers as a symbol of real Indonesia, while Jakarta was represented as a power center that was considered far from reality for days.

That strategy is nothing new in global politics. In modern politics, an approach like this is known as antagonistic popularity, building public solidarity by creating a moral contrast between ordinary people and family.

In Indonesia, the formula works pretty effectively, especially outside the center of Java's urban centers. He created an emotional perception of the closeness between national leaders and grassroots societies. In the age of social media, these kinds of rhetoric have value plus: easily cut into short clips, viral, and easily translated into symbol of conjunction.
But Gorontalo's speech wasn't just about popularity. There are other layers that are more structural.

As a former general, Prabowo consistently looked at the food sector and maritime through the national sovereignty lenses. In that frame of thinking, fishermen are not just small economies, they're part of the strategic defense of the country. The criticism of smart people can actually be read as a criticism of the tecnocratic approach that is considered too far from the real sector.

Visions like this have long roots in modern military traditions: powerful countries must have control over their own food, energy and ocean. And therefore, the rhetoric about fishermen is often connected to larger agendas, self-sustainability, food resistance, and national independence.

It also acts as an instrument of political consolidation at the beginning of government. Almost every new leader requires a narrative of divergence of previous regimes, even when the transition to power is relatively peaceful. In the case of Prabowo, it was interpreted not through a direct attack on the predecessor, but by implicit message:

The irony is that the antielite narrative came from a president who supported the political, military, and very powerful business. But that kind of contradiction often does not become a hindrance in modern popularity. That determines not structural consistency, but emotional effectiveness.

It consistently uses sharp contrast: center versus area, strong versus weak, elite versus people. In fact, Pabowo is a cosmopolitan figure with international education and global experience. The black-and-white contract is not intellectual limitation, it's a deliberate rhetorical choice.

Simple language is easier to create collective identity. It reduces political complexity into a vast public-understood conflict. In modern mass communication, simplicity is often more effective than academic precision.
Hee Prabwo is not anti-intellectual. It's an elite who understands how to speak in anti-elite, and do it well enough that it feels authentic.

Phenomena like this one has many global presedents. In various countries, from Latin America to Eastern Europe, there was a model of leadership by several political scientists referred to as the popularity oligarchic: elite who use antielite rhetoric to maintain mass legitimacy.

In the end, the most important question is not whether Gorontalo's speech is sincere. Politics has always been a performative element. What's more relevant is whether the rhetoric translates into concrete policy.
Is the price of solar for a fishing boat really down. Whether logistics distribution is improving. Whether the welfare of the coast is increasing.
Speech can build public emotion in a day. But long-term political legitimacy is determined by the results that society can feel.
Doctor. Hanny Per
